issues.legal_issue: The authority empowered to establish a market may disestablish it and establish it at another place.
material_facts: A previously functioning market was replaced by a designated market at a different place, and traders challenged the move.
The governing legislation empowered the authority to establish principal and subsidiary markets, and the statutory scheme contemplated changes to those markets over time.
issues.conclusion: The power to establish a market included the power to close an existing market and establish a market elsewhere.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 5 of the Maharashtra Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1963, read with sections 14 and 21 of the Maharashtra General Clauses Act, the Director could close an existing market and establish it elsewhere. The Court approved Bapubhai Ratanchand Shah v. State of Bombay, which applied the general-clause power to exercise a statutory power from time to time and to amend or rescind notifications. A contrary construction would frustrate the statutory purpose as markets may become unsuitable or inconvenient.

predicates.market_relocation_challenge: A proceeding challenges the authority's replacement of an existing market with a market at another place.
predicates.authority_established_a_market: The authority had established a market under the governing market-regulation scheme.
predicates.authority_designated_a_replacement_marke: The authority designated another place to serve as the market.

issues.definition: When a proceeding challenges the replacement of an established market, and the authority established a market and designated a replacement, the replacement is within the authority's power.

issues.legal_issue: A rule requiring marketing of declared agricultural produce to take place only in designated markets is within the rule-making authority and is not inconsistent with the licensing provision.
material_facts: Traders were directed to conduct regulated wholesale business only in designated principal or subsidiary markets.
The applicable rule barred marketing declared agricultural produce elsewhere in the market area, while the statute made licensing subject to rules regulating marketing in that area.
issues.conclusion: The rule was within the rule-making authority, consistent with the statute, and reasonable.
issues.legal_principle: Section 60 of the Maharashtra Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1963 authorised rules to carry out the Act's purposes. Section 6 was expressly subject to rules regulating marketing in the market area, so it applied both before and after markets were established and did not conflict with the rule prescribing where marketing must occur. The Court also relied on the Act's scheme of regulated markets and on Kewal Krishan Puri v. State of Punjab for the need to confine effective supervision to specified places.

predicates.challenge_to_market_only_rule: A proceeding challenges a rule requiring regulated marketing to occur only in designated markets.
predicates.rule_confines_marketing_to_designated_ma: The rule directs persons to conduct regulated marketing in designated markets rather than elsewhere in the market area.
predicates.statute_makes_licensing_subject_to_marke: The governing scheme makes licensing subject to rules that regulate where marketing may occur.

issues.definition: A challenged market-only rule is valid and consistent when it confines regulated marketing to designated markets and the statutory licensing scheme is subject to marketing rules.

issues.legal_issue: Regulation of agricultural produce may extend to trader-to-trader resales and produce brought into a market area from elsewhere while it retains its character as agricultural produce.
material_facts: Traders argued that the regulatory scheme covered only sales by producers to traders and did not cover trader-to-trader transactions or produce imported into the market area.
The scheme regulated marketing, provided services and facilities to traders as well as producers, and included controls over transactions and movement of agricultural produce.
issues.conclusion: The regulation was not limited to a producer's first sale and could cover subsequent transactions, including trader-to-trader transactions and produce brought into the market area from elsewhere.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that marketing includes subsequent transactions in the commodity's movement toward the consumer while the commodity retains its character as agricultural produce. Restricting regulation to producer sales would permit circumvention and undermine effective control. It relied on Mohammadbhai Khudabux Chhippa v. State of Gujarat and Ram Chandra Kailash Kumar & Co. v. State of U.P., which recognised the need to control trader-to-trader transactions and transactions involving produce from outside the market area; it also referred to the Shirname Committee's recommendations. The proviso to Rule 5 was read as dealing with cases otherwise within the main rule, not as creating a distinction between first sales and resales.

predicates.challenge_to_scope_of_market_regulation: A proceeding disputes whether a market-regulation scheme applies to particular transactions in agricultural produce.
predicates.produce_retains_agricultural_character: The produce remains agricultural produce during the transactions at issue.
predicates.transactions_include_resales_or_outside_: The transactions include resales between traders or produce brought into the market area from elsewhere.

issues.definition: When a proceeding disputes the scope of regulation, the produce retains its agricultural character, and the transactions include resales or outside-area supply, the regulation covers those transactions.

issues.legal_issue: Requiring sales and purchases of agricultural produce, including trader-to-trader transactions, to occur in designated markets is not an excessive restriction on the right to carry on trade.
material_facts: The challenged requirement confined marketing transactions to designated markets.

The Court found that dispersing traders across the market area would make supervision difficult, increase the resources required for control, and reduce the availability of market facilities and effective competition for producers.
The market system provided services and facilities that benefited traders as well as producers and consumers.
issues.conclusion: The requirement that transactions occur in the market was not harsh or an excessive restriction on the right to carry on trade.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the constitutional protection of the right to carry on trade and held that localising transactions in markets was helpful and necessary for regulation, control, supervision, and provision of facilities. It reasoned that effective control was less practicable if traders were dispersed throughout a market area and that the market system served traders as well as producers and consumers.

predicates.challenge_to_trade_restriction: A proceeding challenges a requirement affecting where a person may conduct trade in regulated produce.
predicates.regulated_transactions_confined_to_marke: The requirement confines regulated transactions to designated markets.
predicates.market_localization_enables_effective_co: Concentrating transactions in designated markets makes supervision, control, or provision of market facilities more effective.

issues.definition: A restriction confining regulated transactions to markets is not excessive when market localization enables effective control.

issues.legal_issue: A large market area and a single market within it are not unreasonable where the location and surrounding circumstances support the market's public purpose and practical use.
material_facts: Traders challenged the declaration of a large market area and the establishment of a single market serving that area as unreasonable and inconvenient.

The existing markets were congested, and the replacement location was less congested, accessible by major roads and near railway links, and closer to a substantial part of the population and trading community.
issues.conclusion: There was nothing unreasonable in declaring the large area as a market area or establishing a single market for it at the selected location.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the reasonableness of the market-area declaration and market location in light of the public interest, congestion at existing markets, accessibility, transport connections, and the location of residents and traders. On those circumstances, it found no basis to invalidate the declaration or the single-market arrangement.

predicates.challenge_to_market_area_or_location: A proceeding challenges the size of a market area or the location of a market serving it.
predicates.existing_markets_are_congested: The existing markets are overcrowded or otherwise impracticable for their intended use.
predicates.replacement_market_has_practical_access_: The replacement market offers practical advantages such as less congestion or better transport access.

issues.definition: A challenged market area and location are not unreasonable when existing markets are congested and the replacement market has practical access advantages.

issues.legal_issue: Natural justice does not require authorities to invite and hear objections before making a legislative declaration establishing a market yard.
material_facts: A market yard was discontinued at one place and established at another by a government notification.
The challengers argued that the authority should have invited and heard objections before issuing the notification.
The notification activated statutory consequences and was legislative in character.
issues.conclusion: The authority was not required to observe the rules of natural justice by inviting and hearing objections before making the declaration.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished legislative activity from judicial or quasi-judicial decision-making and from administrative action requiring a fair hearing. It relied on Bates v. Lord Hailsham and Tulsipur Sugar Co. v. Notified Area Committee for the principle that natural justice does not ordinarily apply to the making of primary or delegated legislation, including conditional legislation, unless a statute provides otherwise.

predicates.challenge_to_market_yard_declaration: A proceeding challenges a declaration establishing a market yard or changing its location.
predicates.declaration_is_legislative_in_character: The declaration activates statutory consequences and is legislative rather than judicial or quasi-judicial in character.
predicates.no_hearing_requirement_is_provided: The governing scheme does not require objections to be invited and heard before the declaration.

issues.definition: A hearing is not required by natural justice before a challenged market-yard declaration when the declaration is legislative in character and no hearing requirement is provided.

issues.legal_issue: A market should not be notified before it is ready for use, but a notification need not be quashed when adequate facilities and conveniences have since been provided.
material_facts: Traders asserted that the new markets lacked facilities or were not ready when notified.
By the time the Court considered the matter, it was satisfied that reasonable facilities and conveniences were available at the markets.
The traders had repeatedly delayed the operation of the notifications.
issues.conclusion: A place ought not to be notified as a market unless it is ready for use with reasonable facilities, but the Court did not quash the notifications because reasonable facilities and conveniences were then available.
issues.legal_principle: The Court stated that a market should be ready for use with reasonable facilities before notification. It also explained that a notification may be quashed where nothing has been done beyond publishing it; where some necessary facilities remain outstanding, the Court may instead give time-bound directions. On the facts, the available facilities meant quashing was unnecessary.

predicates.challenge_to_market_readiness: A proceeding challenges a market notification on the ground that the market was not ready for use.
predicates.reasonable_facilities_are_now_available: Reasonable facilities and conveniences have been provided at the market by the time the challenge is decided.

issues.definition: A readiness-based challenge does not result in quashing when reasonable facilities and conveniences are available by the time the challenge is decided.

issues.legal_issue: Repeated changes to market-yard notifications are not arbitrary when they were made to give traders time to move to modern market facilities.
material_facts: Notifications concerning the market yards were issued, withdrawn, or changed more than once.
The older markets had existed for a long time, and the government sought to establish modern yards with facilities.
Representations by traders led the government to allow existing markets to continue temporarily so traders could prepare to move.
issues.conclusion: The sequence of notifications was not arbitrary or erratic because it reflected an effort to accommodate traders and give them time to move.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered the history and purpose of the successive notifications and concluded that their apparent inconsistency resulted from the government's effort to accommodate traders during the transition to modern market yards, not from arbitrary or erratic exercise of power.

predicates.challenge_to_repeated_market_notificatio: A proceeding alleges that successive changes to market-yard notifications were arbitrary or erratic.
predicates.changes_allowed_traders_time_to_prepare: The changes allowed traders time to prepare for moving their businesses.
predicates.modern_market_facilities_were_being_prov: The authority was seeking to replace older markets with modern market facilities.

issues.definition: A sequence of changed market notifications is not arbitrary when the changes gave traders time to prepare for a transition to modern market facilities.
